content: Hordeolum, commonly referred to as a stye, is an acute, purulent inflammation of the eyelid margin. It typically arises due to obstruction of the sebaceous gland orifices in the eyelid. This condition can affect sebaceous glands either internally or externally. When the meibomian gland within the tarsal plate is involved, it is classified as an internal hordeolum. Conversely, when the glands of Zeis or Moll, which are associated with eyelash follicles, are affected, it is termed an external hordeolum or stye. The condition is generally self-limiting and often resolves within approximately one week, typically following spontaneous drainage of the abscess. However, in severe cases, the infection can spread to adjacent glands and tissues. Recurrence is a common issue. If an internal hordeolum remains unresolved, it may progress to a chalazion or lead to generalized eyelid cellulitis. Acupuncture, a traditional Chinese medical practice, involves the insertion of fine needles at specific points on the body to treat various diseases. However, the efficacy and safety of acupuncture as a treatment for acute hordeolum remain uncertain. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of acupuncture in treating acute hordeolum compared to no treatment, sham acupuncture, or other active treatments. Additionally, the review aimed to compare the outcomes of acupuncture combined with another treatment versus the other treatment alone. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, PubMed, and others, up to June 7, 2016. Clinical trial registries were also reviewed, and reference lists of potentially eligible studies were examined to identify additional randomized clinical trials (RCTs). The review included RCTs involving individuals diagnosed with acute internal or external hordeola. Studies comparing acupuncture with sham acupuncture, no treatment, or other active treatments, as well as studies comparing acupuncture combined with another treatment versus the other treatment alone, were included. Six RCTs from China, involving a total of 531 participants, were included in the review. The mean age of participants ranged from 18 to 28 years, and approximately 55% of the participants were women. Four RCTs included individuals with initial acute hordeolum lasting less than seven days, one RCT included participants with initial acute hordeolum without specifying the duration, and one RCT included participants with recurrent acute hordeolum with a mean duration of 24 days. Three RCTs included both internal and external hordeolum cases, one RCT focused solely on external hordeolum, and two RCTs did not specify the type of hordeolum. Follow-up in all studies was limited to seven days post-treatment, and no data were available for long-term outcomes. The overall certainty of the evidence was judged to be low to very low, with all RCTs assessed as having a high or unclear risk of bias. The small sample sizes, inadequate allocation concealment, lack of masking of outcome assessors, unclear randomization methods, and high or unreported dropout rates contributed to the low certainty of the evidence. Three RCTs compared acupuncture with conventional treatments. Due to differences in the conventional treatments used across trials, the data were not pooled. One trial found that resolution of acute hordeolum was more likely in the acupuncture group compared to topical antibiotics (32 participants; risk ratio [RR] 3.60; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.34 to 9.70; low-certainty evidence). Another trial reported a higher likelihood of resolution with acupuncture compared to oral antibiotics plus warm compresses (120 participants; RR 1.45; 95% CI 1.18 to 1.78; low-certainty evidence). In contrast, a third trial found little to no difference in resolution when acupuncture was compared to topical antibiotics plus warm compresses (109 participants; RR 1.00; 95% CI 0.96 to 1.04; low-certainty evidence). One RCT reported no adverse events associated with acupuncture. Three RCTs compared acupuncture combined with conventional treatments (topical antibiotics and warm compresses in two RCTs, topical antibiotics alone in one RCT) versus conventional treatments alone. One trial, with very low-certainty evidence, did not report resolution rates but suggested that symptom relief might be higher in the combined treatment group (60 participants; RR 1.80; 95% CI 1.00 to 3.23). A pooled analysis of the remaining two RCTs, with low-certainty evidence, indicated that resolution rates were slightly higher in the combined treatment group compared to the conventional treatment alone group at seven-day follow-up (210 participants; RR 1.12; 95% CI 1.03 to 1.23; I² = 0%). None of the three RCTs reported adverse outcomes. Four participants, two from the acupuncture plus conventional treatments group and two from the conventional treatments alone group, withdrew due to symptom exacerbation. In conclusion, low-certainty evidence suggests that acupuncture, either alone or in combination with conventional treatments, may offer short-term benefits for treating acute hordeolum compared to conventional treatments alone. However, the evidence is limited by methodological weaknesses, small sample sizes, and the lack of long-term follow-up. All included RCTs were conducted in China, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to non-Chinese populations. Additionally, the absence of a valid sham acupuncture control in the included studies raises the possibility of an expectation or placebo effect. Adverse effects of acupuncture were rarely reported, and when mentioned, they were infrequent. Further high-quality RCTs with better methodology, longer follow-up periods, and conducted in diverse populations are needed to provide more robust evidence regarding the efficacy and safety of acupuncture for acute hordeolum.
